title: The Design Space of Tri-Modal Masked Diffusion Models
abstract: Discrete diffusion models have emerged as strong alternatives to autoregressive language models, with recent work initializing and finetuning a base unimodal model for bi-modal generation. Diverging from previous approaches, we introduce the first tri-modal Masked Diffusion Models (MDM) pretrained from scratch on text, image-text, and audio-text data. We systematically analyze multimodal scaling laws, modality mixing ratios, noise schedules, batch-size effects and provide optimized inference sampling defaults. title: Code-Switching Detection via Language-Selective Dimensions in Speech Foundation Models
abstract: Code-switching (CS), the alternation between languages within an utterance, is common in multilingual speech but underrepresented in pretraining corpora. Increasing CS coverage requires finding relevant utterances in large speech collections so that they can be included in training data. One way to find such utterances is to transcribe the speech and detect language alternation in the text, but this depends on obtaining accurate multilingual transcriptions. We propose a lightweight method that detects CS directly from speech. It uses frame-level language information in pretrained speech…

title: Measuring the Impact of Personalized Recommendations
abstract: By Kevin Zielnicki, Guy Aridor, Aurélien Bibaut, Allen Tran, Winston Chou, and Nathan Kallus Introduction Personalization is everywhere on the internet. It shapes the products we discover, the stories we read, the music we hear, and the movies and TV shows we watch. At Netflix, personalization has been central to the member experience for decades — from the Netflix Prize to our modern recommender system that helps members navigate a large and constantly changing catalog. But personalization is not only an algorithmic problem, it is also a measurement problem. How do we know how much value personalization creates? More precisely, how do we separate the appeal of a title from the value created by recommending that title to the right member at the right time? In a new article in the International Journal of Industrial Organization — which we are also presenting at this year’s ACM Conference on Economics & Computation (EC ‘26) — we develop a model of member behavior, title choice, and personalized recommendations. The model lets us estimate how recommendations affect both whether members choose to watch and, if so, which titles they choose. In this post, we summarize our approach and main findings. The Measurement Challenge A natural first attempt at valuing recommendations is to ask: what share of viewing comes from titles that were recommended? This is an intuitive metric, but it fails to answer the causal question at hand. The problem is that recommendations are not randomly assigned. A title appears on a member’s homepage precisely because the recommender system predicts that the member might want to watch it. If a member watches that title, was it because the recommendation caused the member to watch it? Or would she have watched it anyway because of her underlying preference for that kind of title? This is the core measurement challenge: recommendations are targeted to demand, so viewing a recommended title combines the effect of personalization with the member’s underlying preferences. One way to solve this would be to run a large experiment that replaces Netflix’s personalized experience with an unpersonalized one. That would create clean variation — but it would also be a poor member experience. Personalization is a central part of how members locate valuable titles in a large catalog, so turning it off broadly is not an acceptable measurement strategy. Instead, we take a hybrid approach. We build a behavioral model that separates members’ underlying preferences from the incremental effect of recommendations. The model uses the natural variation in the recommendation system, for example due to algorithmic exploration, to estimate how recommendations affect choice. Then, to validate the model predictions about title substitutability, we use small-scale A/B tests that “nudge” the salience of a handful of titles exogenously, generating ground-truth substitution patterns for a subset of titles. This lets us combine the scale and richness of modeling with the credibility of experimental evidence. A Model of Member Choice To measure the value of personalization, we need a model of what members would watch under different recommendation systems. Our model treats Netflix viewing as a day-by-day choice process. On each day, a member chooses among the titles available in the catalog, or she chooses not to watch anything. This gives us a concrete target to estimate: the probability that a member watches each title on a given day, as a function of their preferences, their viewing history, and the recommendations they see. A simple version of this model would be too restrictive. It might assume, for example, that removing one title from the catalog shifts viewing toward all other titles in roughly proportional ways. But that isn’t how member choice works. If a member is considering a romantic comedy, the closest substitutes are likely other romantic comedies, not every title on Netflix equally. title: DataJunction as Netflix’s answer to the missing piece of the modern data stack
abstract: by Olek Gorajek , Samuel Redai , Yian Shang Intro Our Netflix journey from data to dashboards, particularly within the space of the experimentation platform, always presented a unique set of challenges. This blog post aims to illuminate these hurdles and explain how an innovative open-source metric platform became instrumental in overcoming some of them. We’ll showcase the critical role that DataJunction played in streamlining our data workflows and enhancing our ability to derive meaningful insights from our vast datasets. Metrics are the foundation of data-driven decision-making, but at many organizations, they are scattered, inconsistently defined, and difficult to discover or trust. At Netflix, this challenge first became apparent in our experimentation platform, where reliable metrics are essential for interpreting test results. But the complexity of the original tooling made it very difficult to understand and introspect these metrics both in terms of their definitions as well as their values. Initial Problem Scattered metric definitions, redundant datasets, and pipelines are often a natural effect of a fast-moving company with a large and powerful analytical workforce. This is a common problem in big data-driven firms, and it is not easy to solve across multiple departments, which are often governed by somewhat different rules and regulations. An easy-to-use, well-governed, and centralized semantic layer can help with these issues. Our initial problem was most evident in our Experimentation Platform team, where the previous system required: extensive business knowledge familiarity with experimentation conventions and complex engineering practices This led to metric authoring processes that would take weeks, which was a prohibitive requirement for Data Scientists and Analytics Engineers who wanted to onboard new metrics to the Experimentation Platform. Enter DataJunction To address this problem and to set ourselves on the path to a successful semantic layer solution in the future, we looked at several candidates. Among other solutions we evaluated Mando (an internal framework), Minerva (an open source semantic layer from AirBnB), and DataJunction (another open source solution, “DJ” for short). All of them had some strength, but DJ offered one thing that the others did not at the time: a solid SQL parsing and SQL generation engine. At the time of the POC, DJ was also the only open-source solution that stored all its definitions in a connected graph, similar to how relational databases store metadata on their views and queries. Easy “SQL wrangling” with rich metadata was the main feature that convinced us to try it for our immediate use case. DataJunction originated from a similar internal Facebook project created (around 2015) by the data science and infrastructure (DSI) team, mainly as an answer to the need for metrics portability. During several iterations of the Deltoid project — which was the main experimentation platform at Facebook at the time — users were required to rebuild and repopulate their metrics when they wanted to move to the next version of Deltoid. But after implementing DJ and abstracting all metric definitions the team offered seamless migrations by separating the concerns between the metrics and the stats computation platform. That project was subsequently renamed to MDF (Metrics and Dimensions Factory) and promoted as a generic semantic layer used widely by various departments. In 2021, one of the Facebook engineers ( Beto Dealmeida ), started the DJ Github project and built out some basic functionality. Then together with some folks at Netflix expanded the scope further, and soon after that the project was introduced at Netflix. Following that introduction, three Netflix engineers (authors of this blog) together with a couple of external contributors, most notably Nick Ouellet , have been building out the remaining features of the platform. title: Reliable GPU compute for large training & inference jobs
abstract: Authors: Nick Rutigliano , Argha C , Samartha Chandrashekar How we detect failing GPUs and network fabric, remediate machines automatically, and let long-running jobs survive hardware loss. Open Netflix, and the home screen is assembled for you: which rows appear, the order they appear in, the titles within them, and the artwork for each title are chosen by machine learning models trained on how hundreds of millions of members watch. Personalization is one of the most widely used things we build, and members feel it every time they open the app. Like a growing share of Netflix, it runs on GPUs, which train those models and increasingly serve them live. Those GPUs have to stay healthy for that experience to hold up, and keeping them healthy is harder than it sounds. A single large training job can run for weeks across hundreds of GPUs spread over many machines. It runs as a gang: the ranks move in lockstep, exchanging data every step, so the job advances only as fast as its slowest participant and stops entirely if one participant dies. Every GPU, every high-speed network adapter, and every interconnect must keep working throughout the run. At the scale at which modern machine learning runs, individual GPUs and network links can fail during a run, so the underlying platform must be prepared for this and handle it without a person in the loop. This post describes how we keep our GPU infrastructure healthy for training and inference. We cover how we detect failing hardware before and during jobs, how we automatically remediate a bad machine, and how we let a long job survive the loss of a machine. These training workloads run on our modern Kubernetes-native Compute platform. Why GPU reliability matters Netflix aims to entertain the world, and machine learning has been part of how we do that for years, from the recommendations that help members find something to watch to the systems that help produce and promote titles. As generative AI advances, we are investing in it on both sides of the business: for members, through better recommendations and higher-quality promotional assets; and for storytelling, through creative tools for our production partners. All of this runs on GPUs, for both training and inference, and GPU capacity is among the fastest-growing and most expensive parts of our infrastructure. That makes reliability a business concern on two fronts. — - Availability: a training run that loses a machine, or an inference service that cannot get healthy capacity, delays work that members and creators depend on. Cost efficiency: a GPU sitting idle behind a slow neighbor, or a whole machine pulled from the pool because one device is degraded, becomes capacity we paid for and are not using. Higher reliability and higher utilization mean more useful work per GPU, which is equivalent to spending less to do the same work. Inference is a growing share of that GPU footprint as more of these AI features reach members, so the reliability and efficiency that matter for multi-week training runs increasingly matter for always-on serving too. Why basic health checks are not enough We start from the baseline provided by the cloud provider. Cloud providers run instance status checks on virtual machines: a system status check for the underlying host’s power, network, and hardware reachability; an instance status check to verify that the operating system is up and reachable; and a check on attached storage. It emits scheduled maintenance events when it plans to retire or reboot a host, and it can automatically recover an instance that becomes impaired. We use all of these, and the maintenance events feed one of our own checks. They catch a machine that is down, unreachable, or slated for maintenance, and they stop at the instance level. They confirm the box is up and reachable. They do not verify that each GPU, its on-chip memory, its interconnect, and its network fabric are healthy enough to support distributed training. title: Analyzing technical documents with Deep Review
Running Apache Spark experiments in my sleep (and on a plane)
abstract: By Prashanth Gedde Narayanaswamy As one of Netflix’s largest and critical data pipelines, member-sessionizer consolidates tens of billions of hourly client events, encompassing user taps, playbacks, and engagement signals, into individual viewing sessions per profile. A quick two-week tuning effort spiraled into two months when standard approaches hit a wall. Because the failures only happened at full production scale, each test took hours, limiting me to just three or four attempts daily. The turning point was changing the goal: instead of trying to speed up a single run, I built a way to run and monitor multiple tests at once and track every result. That mindset led to an unconventional setup: kicking off five Spark jobs at once and monitoring them over spotty inflight Wi-Fi during a day-long trip home, while cloud servers handled the actual heavy lifting. This post covers how I set up that loop, along with the Spark bottlenecks and memory quirks I uncovered along the way. The Scale Dilemma: Small Samples Don’t Catch Scale Bugs Standard engineering wisdom says that you should isolate bugs on small datasets to iterate quickly. That works for standard software bugs, but it fails completely for big data performance bottlenecks. While upgrading our sessionization pipeline from a legacy logging architecture to a modern platform, the new job hit critical failures, including executor Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors, severe shuffle spillage, and thousands of stage retries. None of these issues could be reproduced using sampled data. The failures only triggered at full production scale because of data skew: an idle Netflix tab left streaming overnight generates tens of thousands of telemetry events, while a typical session only produces a handful. A standard 1% sample misses these extreme long-tail sessions entirely. To catch the real bugs, every test run had to execute against a full hour of unsampled production data, along with all the deployment overhead that came with it. The Strategy: Branch-Driven Isolation The biggest win came from a feature in Dataflow , Netflix’s command-line tool for building, testing, and deploying data pipelines. It supports branch-driven development : our workflows run on Maestro ( Netflix’s workflow orchestrator), which schedules and executes the jobs, and they already use a sanitized branch name (the ${dataflow.sanitizedbranch} placeholder). So if I push a branch like pgn/cap-experiment , then the deployed workflow, its tables, and its run namespace all get tagged with that branch name. This eliminates collisions with team members or between my own concurrent runs. With that isolation in place, the model was simple: one branch is one independent experiment . I parameterized the scheduler (cap size, shuffle partitions, heavy-device threshold, feature flags) and gave each variant its own branch and output table. Instead of queuing five sequential tests over 10 hours, I fired off five variants simultaneously against the same time window. Total execution time dropped from the sum of all runs to just the length of the single slowest job. Managing per-branch tables added zero overhead. Dataflow provisions and updates tables automatically from declared schemas without manual DDL. Whenever I modified the event bag structure between experiments, the table schema updated seamlessly, no CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE required. The only real constraint was cluster contention. Because these heavy Spark jobs shared resources with the rest of the company, peak hours sometimes limited me to two concurrent runs instead of five. But even running two or three jobs in parallel was a massive improvement over single-threaded debugging. The key takeaway: don’t focus on making a single multi-hour run faster, build a setup where you can run many experiments simultaneously without them stepping on each other. Jeva: System One Models from First Principles
abstract: System one models enable direct, low-latency decision-making. Yet recent practice of predicting an answer from serialized text does not, by itself, respect the structure of a decision problem. We argue that current designs underemphasize four important structural requirements. (i) null-aware: Models should distinguish answer absence from uncertainty among candidates; (ii) permutation-invariant: Reordering alternatives should not change the decision; (iii) option-scalable: Growing candidate sets should not require redefining the output space; (iv) cacheable: Request-independent computation over recurring alternatives should be reusable across requests. We introduce Jeva, a decision-native architecture that addresses these requirements jointly. A shared encoder independently represents the request and each option, while a compact decision stack refines only the request state against immutable option memory. Symmetric aggregation yields permutation-equivariant probabilities; shared scoring accommodates variable-size candidate sets. A separate coverage estimate distinguishes answer absence from candidate competition, enabling explicit null outcomes. Request-independent option representations and layer projections support reuse across newly assembled sets. These mechanisms unify Choice, Noul, and Score outputs. Across evaluations, Jeva combines strong typed-decision performance with near-perfect null detection and no decision flips under any tested permutations. It scales to thousands of candidates and substantially reduces latency through cross-request reuse without changing decisions.
